learning_objective: 🎯 Discover Lists: Python's incredibly flexible, mutable data structure that lets you store and manage collections of items!

main_concepts.simple_explanation: A list is an ordered collection of items enclosed in square brackets `[]`. A single list can hold mixed data types (integers, strings, floats) at the same time!
Unlike strings, lists are mutable. This means you can change, add, or remove elements after the list has been created (e.g., `my_list[0] = 100` is perfectly valid).
Just like strings, list elements are accessed using 0-based indexing. You can also slice lists to get a smaller sub-list using the `[start:stop:step]` syntax.
Common methods include `.append()` (adds an item to the end), `.insert()` (adds an item at a specific index), `.pop()` (removes an item), and `.sort()` (arranges items in order).
A list can contain another list as its element (e.g., `[[1, 2], [3, 4]]`). This is often used to represent matrices or 2D grids.

fun_activity.title: 🛒 The Smart Shopping Cart
fun_activity.instructions: Imagine your shopping cart is a Python list: `cart = ["Apples", "Milk"]`. Write the Python command to add "Bread" to the end of the list, and then write the command to remove "Milk"!

exam_tips: 📌 Remember the crucial difference: `.append()` adds a single element to the end, while `.extend()` adds multiple elements from another list.
📌 `.pop()` removes and returns the item at a given index, while `.remove()` deletes the first matching value it finds.
📌 A string is immutable (cannot be changed), but a list is mutable (can be changed in place).
quick_recap: ⭐ Elements in a list are separated by commas and enclosed in `[]`.
⭐ You can use the `+` operator to join two lists together and `*` to repeat a list.
⭐ The `len()` function works on lists to tell you how many elements it contains.
